  - paragraph: "Four trends published in the SPC's 2026 Sustainable Packaging Trends Report define the expected forward trajectory:"
  - paragraph: SCOPE
  - paragraph: "Trend 1 — Packaging Design: Regions are formalizing definitions of recyclability."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "Trend 1 — Packaging Design: Regions are formalizing definitions of recyclability."
    - text: "The report identifies that guidance on recyclability and sustainability is increasingly being defined by Producer Responsibility Organizations (PROs) in the context of EPR. The report states: \"Around the world, regions are beginning to formalize definitions for 'recyclable' and 'sustainable.'\""
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "Trend 2 — Innovation: Healthcare and OTC packaging are catching up to sustainability demands."
    - text: A 2025 Systemiq and Eunomia report, cited in the Trends Report, found that in a business-as-usual scenario, "plastic waste, GHG emissions and costs could grow by 35–40% by 2040." Applying circular economy levers can, the Trends Report states, "cut plastic use by up to 53%, GHG emissions by up to 55%, and system costs by up to 24% by 2040."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "Trend 3 — Policy: EPR is maturing toward industry-regulatory equilibrium."
    - text: The Trends Report describes the industry as being "five years into EPR laws being proposed, passed, and entering early implementation." It states that companies "know enough to plan and act" and should plan for packaging fees to "increase significantly, particularly for difficult-to-recycle materials."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "Trend 4 — Recovery: Data-sharing is creating recyclability clarity under EPR."
    - text: The Trends Report identifies that "success stories of beverage cups and the promising pipeline of new recyclability for PE tubes, PET thermoforms, and small-format plastics prove that when industry players share data, recyclability isn't just a label — it's a trackable, reachable reality."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "How2Recycle film label evolution:"
    - text: "SPC released research at the conference exploring how the How2Recycle label suite can evolve to reflect film collection pathways beyond retailer drop-off bins, including municipal drop-off sites and mail-back or subscription services. The SPC press release states: \"The updated label will continue to be refined and developed in the coming months.\""

  - paragraph: Client talking points
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "What the workspace can credibly say:"
  - list:
    - listitem: The SPC's 2026 Trends Report and SPC Impact 2026 conference confirm that EPR implementation in the US is moving from policy design into operational reality, with Oregon and Colorado having published approved program plans. This is a FACT, sourced from SPC primary research published April 2026.
  - list:
    - listitem: Recyclability definitions are being formalized by PROs under EPR — meaning that a packaging format's "recyclable" claim is increasingly assessed against actual collection, sortation, and end-market performance data, not just technical recyclability. This is a material shift from prior industry practice.
  - list:
    - listitem: California SB 343 is creating reclassification risk for previously assumed-recyclable formats, including molded fiber and polycoated paper.
  - list:
    - listitem: The How2Recycle film label is under active redesign to reflect expanded film recovery pathways; the existing label infrastructure is evolving.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: "Pitfalls to avoid:"
  - list:
    - listitem: Do not assert specific EPR fee figures for any US state without obtaining them directly from the relevant PRO or program plan document. The SPC Trends Report references fee ranges in Oregon and Colorado but specific figures are not reproduced in the source materials available for this brief.
  - list:
    - listitem: Do not characterize compostable packaging as a compliant California alternative without confirming the current status of AB 1201 and NOP rules with counsel. The BPI executive director's description at SPC Impact 2026 — that the framework has "the right ingredients, but the wrong recipe" — signals active legal uncertainty, not resolution.

  - list:
    - listitem:
      - strong: The corporate disclosure core.
      - text: CSRD, EU Taxonomy, Directive (EU) 2025/794 (which pushes back CSRD/CSDDD application dates), GRI Standards, USGBC LEED, and research/market items from Carbon Trust, Cranfield, Fraunhofer IML, and OECD sit together on CSRD sustainability reporting + Scope 3 emissions reporting + supplier data requests.       - strong: The California ISSB-aligned climate-risk axis.
      - text: "Two of the three pivots are California instruments:"
      - strong: SB 261 — Climate-Related Financial Risk Act
      - text: (centrality 13.1) and
      - strong: SB 253 — Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act
      - text: (centrality 12.6), joined by AB 1305. The edge basis scores this pair at 1.0, "grounded in the same source," both touching ISSB disclosure, supplier data requests, and Scope 1 emissions reporting — the tightest same-source cluster in the data.

      - strong: The CBAM/carbon-border cluster.
      - text: EU CBAM and its 2025/2083 amendment score 1.0 on shared carbon border adjustment, CBAM declarations, and ETS allowance surrender tags.     - listitem:
      - strong: The supply-chain due-diligence periphery.
      - text: The conflict-minerals lineage (Regulation (EU) 2017/821 and its two delegated regulations, 2019/429 and 2020/1588) and the forced-labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 connect to the CSRD core only through Directive (EU) 2025/794's CSDDD linkage — obligated mostly on importer/manufacturer or producer, freight forwarder appearing on just one of the four.

The connection engine binds it on shared reporting and emissions scenarios: Scope 3 emissions reporting (35 of 57), CSRD sustainability reporting (27), Scope 1 emissions reporting (17), supplier data requests (14), and import customs declarations (14). Obligated parties skew toward the forwarder's own compliance desk: freight forwarder (45 of 57), shipper (26), importer (19), manufacturer or producer (11), warehouse operator (8). The structure inside it The corporate disclosure core. CSRD, EU Taxonomy, Directive (EU) 2025/794 (which pushes back CSRD/CSDDD application dates), GRI Standards, USGBC LEED, and research/market items from Carbon Trust, Cranfield, Fraunhofer IML, and OECD sit together on CSRD sustainability reporting + Scope 3 emissions reporting + supplier data requests. Two of the three pivots are California instruments: SB 261 — Climate-Related Financial Risk Act (centrality 13.1) and SB 253 — Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act (centrality 12.6), joined by AB 1305. The edge basis scores this pair at 1.0, "grounded in the same source," both touching ISSB disclosure, supplier data requests, and Scope 1 emissions reporting — the tightest same-source cluster in the data. The CBAM/carbon-border cluster. EU CBAM and its 2025/2083 amendment score 1.0 on shared carbon border adjustment, CBAM declarations, and ETS allowance surrender tags. Mexico SEMARNAT and Carbon Trust's global overview (which carries a CBAM declarations tag) sit adjacent, with Regulation (EU) 2024/1157 on waste shipments contributing the ETS allowance surrender overlap. The supply-chain due-diligence periphery. The conflict-minerals lineage (Regulation (EU) 2017/821 and its two delegated regulations, 2019/429 and 2020/1588) and the forced-labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 connect to the CSRD core only through Directive (EU) 2025/794's CSDDD linkage — obligated mostly on importer/manufacturer or producer, freight forwarder appearing on just one of the four. The US state/regional environmental-agency patchwork. Missouri DNR, Clark County, Iowa DNR (the third pivot, centrality 8.6), Colorado DOT, Alaska DOT, West Virginia, Wyoming DEQ, LA Dept. of Building, EPA Michigan, and California Energy Commission bind on Scope 1 emissions reporting plus drayage/urban truck zones and warehouse operator — a real sub-cluster: Clark County–Missouri DNR, Clark County–Iowa DNR, Iowa DNR–LA Dept. of Building. The packaging EPR side-strand. EU PPWR 2025/40, EcoEnclose Blog, Packaging Material Input Costs, SPC Impact 2026, the Polish GIOŚ framework, and the England & Wales 2015 energy-efficiency regs bind on packaging EPR registration and packaging recyclability design (EcoEnclose–PPWR, Polish GIOŚ–PPWR).
